pedagogy.summary: This is a vocabulary/naming topic: children learn the eight planets in order from the Sun and the core space nouns (planet, star, sun, moon, satellite, orbit, solar system, galaxy, universe, asteroid, comet), and use them correctly to describe what is in the sky. It is best taught by pairing each word with a vivid canonical image and one defining feature, using a memorable mnemonic for planet order, building the load-bearing verb 'orbit' (what goes round what), and explicitly separating the confusable categories — the Sun is a star (not a planet), the Moon is not a planet, stars make their own light while planets shine by reflection.
bestPractices: Anchor each term to a canonical image plus one defining feature — a star makes its own light; a planet orbits a star and shines by reflected light; a moon orbits a planet; a comet trails a tail.
Teach planet order with a mnemonic (e.g. 'My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming') and repeated ordering practice, since naming the eight in order is the headline evidence.

Build the nested 'orbit' idea early — moons orbit planets, planets orbit the Sun (a star), the solar system sits within a galaxy — because 'orbit' is the word every later Earth-and-space topic depends on.
Explicitly separate confusable categories: the Sun IS a star, the Moon is NOT a planet, a 'shooting star' is not a star, and asteroids are small/irregular not planets.
Flag that pictures are not to scale (planets are not really crammed together or the same size) so the vocabulary does not smuggle in a scale misconception.
Keep the focus on naming and correct use at this age — defer mechanisms (why things orbit, phases) to later topics.
keyRepresentations: An ordered row of the eight planets out from the Sun, with the Sun labelled as a star.
A nested-orbit picture: Moon → Earth, planets → Sun, solar system within a galaxy within the universe.
Word–picture cards pairing each vocabulary term with an image and one distinguishing feature.
A mnemonic strip for planet order.
commonMisconceptions: The Sun is a planet (it is a star) — or, conversely, the Sun is not a star at all.
The Moon is a planet, rather than a satellite orbiting Earth.
Stars and planets are the same, and a 'shooting star' (a meteor) is a star.
Pluto is still the ninth planet — it was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
Planets are all similar in size and packed close together, a scale error picked up from diagrams.

learn.summary: A space-vocabulary/naming topic for ages 5–8: learn the eight planets in order from the Sun and the core space nouns (planet, star, sun, moon, satellite, orbit, solar system, galaxy, universe, asteroid, comet), and use them correctly to describe what is in the sky. Anchor each word to a canonical image plus one defining feature, lock in planet order with a mnemonic and ordering practice, build the load-bearing verb 'orbit' (what goes round what), and explicitly separate confusable categories — the Sun is a star (not a planet), the Moon is a satellite (not a planet), stars make their own light while planets shine by reflected light. Keep the focus on naming and correct use; defer mechanisms (why things orbit, phases) to later topics.

activities.title: Tap-through solar-system scene with category badges
feedback: When the Sun is tapped, confirm it is a STAR at the centre of our solar system, not a planet.

At the two-dot night-sky panel, name which is a planet and which is a star and give the test: one makes its own light, the other only reflects it (this is revealed by the panel, not judged by looking).
When zooming out, name each nested level in order (solar system, then galaxy, then universe) so the move outward matches the words.
activities.rationale: A naming/vocabulary topic pairs each term with a canonical image and one defining feature; tap-to-reveal lets a child meet each word with its picture and category. The two-dot comparison is intended to make the star/planet distinction clear through the reveal rather than merely stated; it is not a criterion a young child can reliably judge visually.
sourceClaims: DfE Year 5 non-statutory guidance states the Sun is a star at the centre of our solar system with 8 planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), that Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, and that a moon is a body that orbits a planet.
A common category confusion is that the Sun/Moon are treated as fixed or miscategorised and that children conflate stars and planets; correcting category vocabulary is a documented teaching need.
learnerActions: Explore a single richly labelled solar-system scene where tapping each body reveals its name, one memorable feature, and a category badge: planet / star / moon / asteroid / comet.
Tap the Sun to lift a flap that declares 'I'm a star, not a planet'.
Use a lift-the-flap that contrasts how a moon differs from a planet (a moon — also called a natural satellite — orbits a planet; a planet orbits the Sun).
Tap a comet to reveal its name and its defining feature — an icy body that grows a glowing tail when it comes near the Sun — so every target word has a picture-and-feature anchor.
Follow a zoom-out drill-down that travels outward: solar system → Milky Way galaxy → universe, so the nesting words land as places you move out through.
Tap two look-alike dots in a night-sky panel; the panel reveals that one is a planet (shines by borrowed, reflected light) and the other a star (makes its own light).
activities.intendedInsight: Each space word belongs to a specific kind of object, and the key distinction the whole vocabulary hinges on — a star makes its own light, a planet shines by reflected light — is made clear through the tap-reveal comparison of two look-alike dots; it is not something a child can simply judge by eye.

activities.title: Order the planets and sort sky objects
feedback: Snap a planet into place when it is in the correct position; on a wrong placement, say which planet should come next out from the Sun.
When an object is mis-sorted, restate the sorting test for the correct bin (e.g. 'a moon orbits a planet, so the Moon goes in the moon bin, not the planet bin').
activities.rationale: Active naming and sorting with immediate feedback directly rehearse the two evidence goals (order the planets; distinguish planet/star/moon/asteroid); a mnemonic supports recall of the sequence. Placement and sorting rehearse recognition and sequencing; they do not by themselves demonstrate spontaneous correct use.
sourceClaims: DfE Year 5 non-statutory guidance states the Sun is a star at the centre of our solar system with 8 planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), that Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, and that a moon is a body that orbits a planet.
learnerActions: Drag the eight planets into correct order outward from the Sun (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), using a mnemonic such as 'My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming' as a memory aid.

Sort a set of sky objects into bins by category: makes its own light (star), a big, round world that orbits the Sun and shines by borrowed light (planet), orbits a planet (moon), a small rocky body that orbits the Sun, often lumpy in shape (asteroid).
Repeat the ordering until the sequence is secure.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming the eight planets in order and placing each sky object in the right category are the two headline skills, rehearsed through active placement with feedback.

activities.title: Build the nested 'orbit' idea with hands and narration
feedback: If 'orbit' is used to mean 'near' or 'next to', ask the child to show the circling motion with a hand and re-state what goes around what; give more move-and-narrate practice rather than drilling dictionary definitions.
If the Sun is called a planet, contrast light-MAKER (star) with light-BORROWER (planet) and sort a few objects by that test.

If a star and planet, or moon and star, are confused, sort sky objects three ways: makes its own light (star), a big, round world that orbits the Sun and shines by borrowed light (planet), orbits a planet (moon).
activities.rationale: 'Orbit' is the load-bearing verb every later Earth-and-space topic depends on; it is sometimes acquired before its full meaning attaches, so the circling sense is best built through move-and-narrate use rather than recited definitions. This developmental point comes from the assessment notes, not from a cited source.
learnerActions: Show 'orbit' with a hand — move one fist around another and say what is going around what.
Narrate the nesting: the Moon orbits the Earth; the planets orbit the Sun (a star); the solar system sits within a galaxy, within the universe.

Answer probe questions: 'Is the Sun a planet, or something else?'; 'What does the Moon orbit — the Earth or the Sun?' (it orbits the Earth, and travels around the Sun together with the Earth); 'If I said Mars is a moon, would that be right? Why not?'
activities.intendedInsight: 'Orbit' means travelling around, not being near or next to — and the going-around relationships are nested (moon→planet, planet→Sun).

constraints: Keep the focus on naming and correct use at this age; defer mechanisms (why things orbit, phases of the Moon) to later topics.
Diagrams are not to scale — planets are not really the same size or crammed close together. State this explicitly so the vocabulary does not smuggle in a scale misconception.
Pluto is a dwarf planet (reclassified in 2006), not the ninth planet; a 'shooting star' is a meteor, not a star.

Do not drill dictionary definitions of 'orbit'; the goal is correct use in running speech, not reciting definitions. Reciting the planet mnemonic without being able to point-and-apply is rote-without-use.

Sorting bins and drag-to-order give recognition and sequencing practice; they do not by themselves show the child can use the words correctly in spontaneous description — pair with narration where the child walks the model outward and names each body and its motion.
An orbiting 3D model can convey the spatial sense of 'orbit', but naming is fully served in 2D; treat 3D as an optional engagement aid, not a requirement for this naming goal.

Open conversation/role-play does not by itself drill a fixed term set or the planet sequence; for early readers it may be better suited to consolidating vocabulary after the terms have been introduced than to first establishing them.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (IOPSpark teaching-and-learning issues) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim about documented category confusion as unconfirmed.

The source row's 3D-interactive note asserts '3D adds scale and cost without extra naming payoff' and the conversation note asserts an 'open dialogue is the wrong vehicle'; these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements.

The 'light-borrower vs light-maker' sorting test is a sound heuristic for star/planet; the original recommendation also cited planets 'wandering', but this is not reliably perceptible to young learners at a single glance, so it is dropped from the learner-facing two-dot panel and the star/planet distinction there is revealed by the interactive reveal rather than by eye.

Activity 3's 'orbit' rationale derives from the assessment's developmental error pattern, not from either cited source; sourceClaims left empty rather than citing the IOPSpark category-confusion claim, which concerns star/planet conflation, not the meaning of 'orbit'.

The original best practices paired 'comet' with the feature 'trails a tail'; that pairing has now been added to the tap-through scene so every target term has a canonical image+feature anchor. Whether 'comet' should also carry its own sorting-bin/badge category alongside planet/star/moon/asteroid is a design judgement not resolved by the source row.

probeDeeper: You said Jupiter orbits the Sun — show me 'orbit' with your hand. What is moving around what?
Is the Sun a planet, or something else? How is it different from Earth?
The Moon — does it go around the Sun, or around us? How do you know?
If I said 'Mars is a moon,' would that be right? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: In running speech the child names the planets Mercury→Neptune in order, uses 'orbit' for the going-around motion (planets orbit the Sun; the Moon orbits the Earth), calls the Sun a star, a satellite a 'moon', and applies 'asteroid' correctly — reserving each term for the right object rather than reciting definitions.

errorPatterns.pattern: treats the Sun as a planet — 'the Sun is the biggest planet' — because it is a big ball in space
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast light-MAKER (star) with light-BORROWER (planet): the Sun makes its own light, planets only reflect it; sort a few objects by that test.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: labels the Sun a planet while walking the model outward

errorPatterns.pattern: uses 'orbit' to mean 'near/next-to' rather than 'travelling around' — a word acquired before its full meaning attaches
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill dictionary definitions; give more move-and-narrate practice ('show me orbit with your hand — what goes around what?') so the circling sense attaches through use.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says the Moon 'orbits' beside the Earth, or applies 'orbit' to a body's position rather than its motion

errorPatterns.pattern: stars and planets are the same, just dots — 'a moon is a little star'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort sky objects three ways: makes its own light (star), borrows light and orbits the Sun (planet), orbits a planet (moon).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: calls a star a planet or a moon a star while pointing

responseLevels.gap: Recites planet names (often via a mnemonic) but mislabels object types — calls the Sun a planet, uses 'orbit' for position, cannot distinguish star, planet and moon.
responseLevels.full: While describing the model names Mercury→Neptune in order, uses 'orbit' correctly for both planets-round-Sun and Moon-round-Earth, and cleanly distinguishes star, planet, moon and asteroid — transferring the words to a new object when asked 'what would you call…?'
responseLevels.partial: Names the planets in order and uses 'orbit' for the Sun–planet motion, but slips on one relation (e.g. the Moon orbiting the Sun) or one category (asteroid vs planet).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here's a picture of the Sun with lots of things around it. Walk me from the Sun outwards and tell me the story of our solar system — point to each thing, tell me what it is and how it moves.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has the words but not the concepts mislabels while narrating — calls the Sun a planet, says the Sun 'orbits' Earth, or uses 'orbit' to mean 'is near'. A child with secure vocabulary uses each term for the right object and reserves 'orbit' for the circling motion. Reciting the planet mnemonic while being unable to point-and-apply reveals rote-without-use, which a 'define X' question would miss.
